writes `import/staging/accounts.csv`, which a new database's import loads into
`staging.accounts`. Two tables that would be one file there (`core.accounts` and
`staging.accounts`) are refused, named, before anything is written: an import loads each file
there into that schema, so export into the folder, with `-n`, the one table whose rows the file
should hold (outside `import/` — the default `export/` — each table keeps its schema folder). Generated columns are left out of
every export. A database
pinned to another scope is refused before a file is written (`Exporting under another scope would
read tables this database was not built with.`; no `--allow-scope-change`).

CSV/TSV are written as Postgres's `COPY` writes them,
on SQLite too — header row, NULL as an empty field, `''` as `""`, a value holding the delimiter,
a quote or a line break quoted with its quotes doubled — so an export loads back to the same
values on either engine (before 0.25 a SQLite export joined cells unquoted; it now writes the
header even for an empty table). A SQLite BLOB is written as `\x…` lowercase hex, as Postgres
writes a `bytea`, in every format, and read back into a BLOB column (before 0.25 every BLOB came
out NULL). Pointing `-o` at `import` produces a round-trip (CSV, TSV or JSONL): what `export`
writes, `import` reads back under the `import/<schema>/<table>.<fmt>` convention.

A JSONL export writes each row as the JSON Postgres renders, so quotes, backslashes and newlines
load back unchanged, a json column keeps its exact text and a string scalar stays a string. Every
column's key is written, and `null` is SQL NULL for every type; a json/jsonb column holding the
JSON value `null` is written `{"$json": null}` (a value that is itself a one-key `$json` object is
wrapped once more), which the import unwraps one level. (0.24 wrote both NULLs as `null`, from
`COPY` text that also doubled every backslash.) A `json[]`/`jsonb[]` element that is SQL NULL
still comes back as the JSON value `null`.

**Moving a long-lived system.** The pattern: views that dereference each FK back to
the natural key the import staging tables expect, listed under `export:`, so an
export from the old database matches the staging tables and an import into the new
one runs the same procedures as a fresh seed. An import loads a file into the table its folder
and name say, so export the views straight into the staging schema's folder: `dbd export -d $OLD
-o import/staging` (→ `import/staging/lookups.csv`, …), then `dbd deploy -d $NEW`. Name each view
after the staging table it feeds, and its columns after that table's columns (a CSV loads by its
header; the order is free). Not `-o import`: that keeps each view under its own schema's folder
(`import/staging_export/lookups.csv`), which an import refuses as a load into a view. Not needed
when the import files are the well-managed source of truth.

Per-table `export_data` is not available on Convex — `npx convex export` only
supports whole-deployment dumps, so the command errors with that explanation
rather than writing a partial file.

### dbd deploy

One-shot: fetch source → apply → grants → import → policies → cleanup.

`deploy` means "bring the database fully up from source", so RLS policies from
`policies/` are applied **unconditionally** — unlike `dbd apply`, where they are
opt-in behind `--with-policies`. Grants are the same `dbd apply` applies (schema +
target grants, the PostgREST ride-along on `supabase`; under `--scope` only on the
schemas it builds), right after the schema and before import and policies.
`-c/--config` works as on every command.

`deploy` is the only command that accepts a GitHub source; every other command
refuses one with a message (clone the repo and pass its path). For a private
repository set `GITHUB_TOKEN` — sent as a bearer token to `api.github.com` only.
`--dry-run` runs the real deploy's gates (it refuses an unparseable file, a gap, a
closure conflict, a missing hook file, a data file outside `import.staging`, a loader
tie or a loader the scope leaves out) and reports after scope filtering: the `scope 'X': N of M entities` line, `deps:
include` gaps as `+ auto-included:` lines, each hook the scope would skip, the entities
that would be applied, the data files that would be imported with the reason for each
left out (and each `import.after` hook the scope skips), and the policy files that would
be applied and skipped. Given a database it also checks the scope pin, the environment guard
and the version guard and lists the pending migrations, as `apply --dry-run` does. The real deploy checks
the import phase's refusals before it applies anything, so a refusal never leaves the
schema applied and the data not loaded, and reports each phase in the order it ran. Its apply
phase runs `dbd apply`'s guards: a database pinned to another scope, a `-e dev` run on one
marked prod, and a project older than the database are refused before anything runs.

```sh
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database -d $DATABASE_URL
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database@v2.1 -d $DATABASE_URL
dbd deploy --dry-run --source owner/repo/path -d $DATABASE_URL
dbd deploy --scope hub -d $HUB_URL          # deploy only the hub subset
dbd deploy --scope hub --deps include -d $HUB_URL   # auto-include dependencies
dbd deploy --no-cache --source owner/repo/path -d $URL     # re-download this source
dbd deploy --clear-cache --source owner/repo/path -d $URL  # wipe the whole cache first
dbd deploy --adopt-from billing -d $URL                     # as on apply
```

GitHub sources are cached under `~/.cache/dbd` (macOS: `~/Library/Caches/dbd`).
`--no-cache` re-downloads the current source; `--clear-cache` removes the entire
cache directory before deploying. Both are no-ops for local path sources
(`--clear-cache` still clears the cache).

**Nothing is skipped silently.** Every phase reports its count, including zero,
and a deploy that imports nothing says why:

| Reason a data file did not load | Reported as |
| --- | --- |
| No `import/` directory | `no import/ directory — nothing to import` |
| File under `import/<other-env>/` | `N data file(s) under import/<env>/ skipped — this run's env is '<env>'` |
| File in a folder deeper than an import reads | `import/staging/sub/x.csv not loaded — an import reads import/<schema>/<table>.<ext>, or import/<env>/<schema>/<table>.<ext> for env dev or prod, and no folder deeper` |
| Staging file failed to parse | `staging table X not imported — data file failed to parse` |
| Entry cut by `--scope` | `X not imported — T is outside scope '<name>'` |
| A function reads a staging table no procedure loads | `X has no loader procedure — function F reads it but is not run` |
| A procedure reads a staging table it is not the loader of | `P reads X but is not called — L is its loader` |

A policy file that fails is **non-fatal**: it is reported as a warning, counted
in the summary (`N policy file(s) applied, M failed`), and the deploy still
exits 0. This is the wrong-`--env` trap — a deploy that applied DDL but seeded
no rows used to look indistinguishable from a clean success.

`dbd deploy` is a thin wrapper over the library's `Design::deploy`, so the CLI
and an embedding application run the identical pipeline and cannot drift.

### dbd reconcile

Pre-release (pre-v1) **declarative** apply: diff the live database against the
design and apply the difference in place — `CREATE` for new tables, `ALTER` for
changed ones — with **no snapshot files and no version bump**. This avoids
cutting a throwaway snapshot for every schema tweak while the design churns.

```sh
dbd reconcile --dry-run -d $DATABASE_URL              # preview the plan (entity summary)
dbd reconcile --dry-run -v -d $DATABASE_URL           # preview + show the column-level ALTER SQL
dbd reconcile -d $DATABASE_URL                        # apply (create + alter)
dbd reconcile --allow-destructive -d $DATABASE_URL    # also drop columns/constraints
dbd reconcile --prune -d $DATABASE_URL                # also drop orphaned tables
dbd reconcile --prune-unowned -d $DATABASE_URL        # and those nobody owns another project might
```

Add `-v` to a `--dry-run` to print the generated `ALTER` SQL beneath each altered
entity — the exact column-level change, before applying. Like every dry run it creates no
database: given a SQLite file that does not exist, it previews against an empty in-memory one —
what its run would create — and refuses where the run refuses.

Reconcile writes in one pass over the design in the dependency order `apply` uses —
each entity created, altered or re-applied at its place, so a function comes before a
table whose default or trigger calls it — then matview restamps, then prunes. **It is
not one transaction**: each step commits as it runs, so a failing step stops the run
with the steps before it applied; only that step (one table's `ALTER` script, one enum's
recreation — each a single statement batch) rolls back. A batch transaction is not
possible: an enum value added by `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE` cannot be used until its
transaction commits, so a later default or CHECK naming it would fail.

The diff is scoped to the schemas the design declares — reconcile never touches
tables in other schemas. Two kinds of destruction each need an explicit opt-in:
`--allow-destructive` drops a **column**/constraint from a managed table, or
removes an enum **value** (see below) — without it the run refuses, listing each drop by
entity (`app.people: drops column nickname`) and nothing else (before 0.25 it listed every
altered table, ones that had only gained a column included);
`--prune` drops a whole **orphaned table** (in a managed schema, no longer in the
design) that this project owns, or that nobody owns in a schema no other project uses;
another project's table is never dropped, and one nobody owns where another project might is
kept and named (`unowned: app.tmp_report — not dropped because app is shared with "billing"
(--prune-unowned drops it)`). `--prune-unowned`, which implies `--prune`, drops those too,
naming each. Without `--prune`, orphans are reported and left in place. Under
`--scope`, a table the design declares outside the scope is never an orphan — a
scope narrows what is applied, not what the project owns (true from 0.24.1;
earlier releases dropped those tables under `--scope --prune`, #40). On a
`supabase` target Supabase's own schemas are never pruned. `public` is managed only
when the design puts something there — a role or an extension with no `schema:`
does not count (before 0.25 it did, and `--prune` dropped every undeclared table in
`public`). Orphaned
enums are only warned about, never auto-dropped. Reconcile is **disabled once the
project is released** (`project.released: true`) — see `dbd release`; it checks
that flag only. `--dry-run` refuses a database pinned to another scope, as the real
run does, and both refuse a `-e dev` run on a database marked prod. Reconcile records
`project.version` in the bookkeeping row — `0` when the design has none, as `apply`
does — even over a newer database's (the older-project guard covers `apply` and
`deploy`).

**Grants and hooks.** A reconciled database is the one an apply builds, so reconcile runs
the design's `apply.before` and `apply.after` hooks and then its `grants:`, scoped as `apply`
scopes them: `apply.before` after every gate (the `--allow-destructive` refusal included, so a
refused run fires no hook) and before the first write, `apply.after` after the writes and the
pg_cron sync, grants last (`Applied grants.`). A skip is named before the run; `--dry-run` names
it too, refuses a missing hook file, and lists the hooks and grants the run goes on to apply
(`run apply.after sql/realtime.sql`, `grant on app: app_reader (usage, select)`). The summary
counts the hooks:
`Reconciled — 2 created, 0 altered, 3 re-applied, 0 re-stamped, 0 pruned, 3 hook script(s) run.`

Reconcile compares the introspected live schema against the design and
canonicalizes the two representations first: it lifts inline PK/UNIQUE to
structural constraints, schema-qualifies bare enum types (`status` →
`config.status`) and the types an extension installs outside `public` (`citext` →
`extensions.citext`, `vector(384)` → `extensions.vector(384)`) to match
introspection, and normalizes type aliases (`int4` →
`integer`, `timestamptz` → `timestamp with time zone`). It reconciles **columns**
(name/type/collation/nullability/default/identity — a collation change is `ALTER COLUMN …
TYPE … COLLATE`), **PK/UNIQUE** constraints, **foreign keys** (`MATCH FULL`, `DEFERRABLE` and
`INITIALLY DEFERRED` included), **CHECK** and **EXCLUDE** constraints (EXCLUDE in a pass of its
own), **indexes** and **column comments**. What an extension owns is not read from the live
side, so it is never drift nor an orphan.

Everything is matched by shape, never by name — Postgres auto-names what the
design leaves unnamed, so a name difference is not drift. PK/UNIQUE match on their
columns, FKs on (columns, referenced table/columns, actions, MATCH, deferral), CHECKs on the
canonicalized expression, an EXCLUDE on its definition read back through Postgres's grammar,
indexes on (unique flag, access method, ordered columns). The one name read is a key's
backing index, matched by the constraint's name — so an index the design declares over a
key's columns is real, and dropping it from the database is drift (before 0.25 it was taken
for the key's own index, and `diff` stayed empty). A declared object the live DB lacks is added; one the design dropped is
removed (`DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS "<live name>"` / `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS`, gated
behind `--allow-destructive`). Constraint names are read off the live object for
the drop, which is why they survive canonicalization.

Changing which columns a PRIMARY KEY covers is a replacement: the old constraint
is dropped by its real live name and the new one added, in that order, in place on
a table that already holds rows. The new key columns must already be `NOT NULL`
and unique across existing rows or Postgres rejects the `ADD`: that table's `ALTER`
script rolls back (the old key stays) and the run stops, with what earlier steps
wrote left committed. Generated ALTERs run with the managed schemas on
`search_path`, mirroring the DDL files.

**Enum value removal** (`--allow-destructive`). Postgres has no `ALTER TYPE … DROP
VALUE`, so the type is recreated: the managed views that read a table with a column
of the enum — and views over those — are dropped, deepest first; column defaults are
taken off; the type is renamed aside (`<name>__dbd_old`) and recreated with exactly the
declared values in order; each column is moved across with `USING <col>::text::<type>`
(`::text[]` for an array); the defaults are restored; an index that reads the column — a
partial index's predicate, an expression key — is dropped and rebuilt around the swap (left in
place, Postgres re-reads it against the renamed type: `operator does not exist`); the old type is
dropped. Only
views are dropped — tables, functions and procedures that merely reference the table
never are — and the views come back later in the same run, from the pass that
re-applies every managed view. The recreation is one statement batch, so a row
holding the removed value (named by its column and the value), a default naming it, or a
view dbd does not manage fails it whole, naming the object, and stops the run. The enum's
`COMMENT ON TYPE` is carried to the recreated type (before 0.25 it went with the old one).

A **live materialized view reading the column** — directly or through views — blocks the
swap, and dbd never drops one, so reconcile refuses before writing anything, under
`--dry-run` too, exiting non-zero:

```
reconcile cannot remove enum value 'meh' from app.mood: materialized view app.mood_counts reads a column of that type. dbd never drops a materialized view, so nothing was changed. To go on:
  1. drop it by hand: DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW "app"."mood_counts";
  2. re-run `dbd reconcile --allow-destructive`: it removes the value and re-creates, from the design, the materialized views it declares
```

(a third step names a matview the design does not declare, for you to re-create). It is
asked of the database, so a matview already dropped blocks nothing. Before 0.25 it decided
from the design: with a matview over the column declared it planned nothing for the enum,
warned, and exited 0 "Reconciled" — and the re-run its advice led to re-created the matview
and declined again.

### dbd diff

Read-only. Show the complete difference between the live database and the
design — columns (with their collation), PK/unique, foreign keys (their `MATCH FULL` and
deferral too), CHECK and EXCLUDE constraints, indexes, column comments and enums, plus
matview drift. It compares the same model `reconcile` converges (table comments are in
neither); diff changes nothing, works after `dbd release`, and also shows what reconcile
won't touch (orphans without `--prune`, orphan enums, drifted matviews). What an extension
owns is left out of the live side. Under `--scope` it refuses on a dependency gap. On a
database pinned to another scope it says so before the diff — what the pinned scope does
not build reads as missing — and a `--json` diff says it on stderr.

```sh
dbd diff -d $DATABASE_URL              # human report (summary + SQL)
dbd diff -d $DATABASE_URL --json       # structured diff for tooling/CI
dbd diff -d $DATABASE_URL --exit-code  # 0 in sync, 2 on drift, 1 on error
```

The desired schema is parsed from DDL, the live schema introspected; dbd
normalizes representation noise (type aliases plus array and date-time spellings
— `int4`→`integer`, `text[3]`→`text[]`, `time`→`time without time zone`; default
casts, enum and extension-type qualification (`citext`→`extensions.citext`), PK/UNIQUE-backing indexes (matched by the constraint's name, so
a declared index over a key's columns that the database lost is drift), FK `NO
ACTION`/auto-generated names, EXCLUDE spelling, and CHECK-expression spelling via libpg_query — parens/case, `IN` ↔
`= ANY (ARRAY[…])`, literal casts, `BETWEEN` ↔ its `>=`/`<=` expansion, casts on
`ARRAY[…]` constructors, and `AND`/`OR` nesting; a `nextval('s')` default matches
the `nextval('s'::regclass)` Postgres reports) so only real drift shows. An
unparseable CHECK is shown flagged `advisory`. Covers tables + enums
structurally, plus **materialized-view drift** (each matview reported
`missing`/`drifted`/`unstamped`/`orphan` via the `dbd:hash` drift stamp in
`dbd.matview_stamps`; in `--json` as `matview_drift`, and counts toward
`--exit-code`). Views/functions/roles/sequences are not structurally diffed, and
table, view and enum comments are not compared. A pooled connection's inherited
`search_path` can still make a bare `nextval('s')` read as drift now and then.

### dbd release (alias: dbd baseline)

Cut the first version: write a **baseline snapshot** at the current
`project.version` (the anchor future `dbd snapshot` diffs against) and set
`project.released: true`, which locks the project into the snapshot/migration
workflow and disables `dbd reconcile`.

```sh
dbd release --name "v1 GA"   # baseline snapshot + released: true
dbd baseline                 # alias
```

Refuses if the project is already released or the design has entity errors (run
`dbd inspect` first). After release the flow is the ordinary one: edit DDL →
`dbd snapshot` → `dbd apply`. `release` sets the flag by editing `design.yaml` in
place, keeping its comments, blank lines and flow-style lists.

**Snapshots but not released.** `init --from-db` and `merge` write snapshots
without setting `released`. Such a project is on the migration track (snapshot →
apply) but still allows `reconcile`. `dbd release` releases it at the version its
latest snapshot reached, with no second baseline (`--name` is unused); it refuses
while the design has changes no snapshot records (capture them with `dbd snapshot`
first) or when `project.version` disagrees with the latest snapshot.

### dbd snapshot

```sh
dbd snapshot --name "add notes column"
dbd snapshot --list
```

Diffs the current DDL against the latest snapshot and writes a versioned
migration. **Smart multi-snapshot**: complex changes auto-split into safe stages —
a column rename → 2 snapshots (add+copy, drop old), a type change → 2 (add+CAST,
drop old), an enum value removal → 2 (the data mapping, a TODO to fill in; then the type swap —
the type renamed aside and recreated, each column moved across with its views, materialized views,
indexes and default dropped and restored around it, the old type dropped once no column uses it,
its `COMMENT ON TYPE` carried to the new one). Before 0.25 the removal took three stages through
`TEXT`, failed on any view over the column and on an enum default, and lost the type's comment.

`dbd snapshot` writes `project.version` by editing `design.yaml` in place, keeping its
comments and layout.

A table removed from the design is written as `DROP TABLE … CASCADE` in
`migrations/<NNN>/<schema>/<table>.sql`, where every per-table migration goes, and the
next `dbd apply` runs it (a hand-written `<table>.drop.sql` there takes precedence). A
drop runs only where the table still exists, and only a drop that ran is counted. Before
0.25 apply looked only for `<table>.drop.sql`, so a generated drop never ran while the
migration was recorded as applied.

`*.data.sql` corrections run after every schema change of their version, the other
tables' included (CAST heuristics auto-fill type conversions; non-derivable cases like enum
value mapping emit `-- TODO:` comments). These are **gated**: `dbd inspect` surfaces
unresolved TODOs, and `dbd apply`, `deploy` and — given a database — their dry runs refuse
while any remain. How `apply` runs pending versions — one at a time, enum values committed
first — is under [dbd apply](#dbd-apply).

### dbd migrate

```sh
dbd migrate --status   # read-only: local snapshot version vs database version
```

`migrate` is diagnostic only — there is no `--apply`. Pending migrations are
executed by `dbd apply` (it runs DDL + pending migrations together); `dbd apply --dry-run` with a
database configured lists the ones it would run, destructive statements marked `⚠`. A project
older than the database (design v2, database v3, or an unversioned design) is refused by `apply`,
`deploy` and their dry runs rather than re-applying older DDL over a newer schema. A database with
no recorded version shows `Database version: none recorded`; `Database is up to date.`
is printed only when the two versions match — with none pending but the versions apart,
it says why (the next apply records the version; no migration bridges the gap; or the
database is ahead of the latest snapshot). A database pinned to a scope is noted — `note:
this database is pinned to scope 'hub' — it was built with that scope's entities, not the
whole design.` — since the versions are the whole project's.

### dbd policies

```sh
dbd policies                # apply policies/<schema>/<table>.sql (RLS)
dbd policies --dry-run
dbd policies --scope hub    # only policies whose table is in the scope
dbd apply --with-policies   # apply entities + policies in one step
```

Row-Level Security policy files contain idempotent SQL (`enable row level
security`, `drop policy if exists`, `create policy`). Failures are logged and
skipped (fail-forward); exit code 1 if any failed.

`dbd deploy` (and `Design::deploy`) runs this phase unconditionally as its final
step. There, a failed policy file is a warning rather than an error: it is
reported and counted, and the deploy still exits 0.

**Scope.** A policy protects one table, and its target is read from the path —
`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql` names `<schema>.<table>`. Under `--scope`, a
policy whose table is outside the working set is skipped, with the file, target
and scope named, and counted in the deploy summary:

```
Skipped ./policies/dojo/repository_metrics.sql — dojo.repository_metrics is outside scope 'daemon'
```

This matters when one design serves several planes: without it, a policy for a
schema a plane lacks runs anyway and reports `FAILED … schema dojo does not
exist` on every deploy — an expected condition dressed as an error, which is how
real failures stop being read. Runs without `--scope` apply every file.
`dbd policies --dry-run` applies the same filter, listing what would apply and what it
skips under separate headings.

**Scope guard.** `dbd policies` refuses a database pinned to another scope, as `apply`,
`deploy`, `reconcile`, `reset`, `import`, `export` and `refresh` do (`scope guard: this database is pinned to scope
'hub', but you requested 'all'. Applying another scope's policies would secure tables
this database was not built with.`). There is no `--allow-scope-change`: policies never
re-pin, so run under the pinned scope or re-point the database with `dbd apply
--allow-scope-change` first. With a database configured, `policies --dry-run` checks the pin
too, so the preview refuses where the run would; with none configured it lists the files offline.

A file off the `policies/<schema>/<table>.sql` layout has no derivable target and
always applies — scope filtering here is a correctness aid, not a security
boundary.

### dbd combine

```sh
dbd combine -f init.sql
dbd combine --scope hub -f hub.sql      # only the 'hub' scope's working set
dbd combine --scope hub --deps include  # self-contained closure
```

`--scope`/`--deps` filter the combined SQL to the working set (filter-only, no gap gate) and print the scope line. Roles are kept in every scope; extensions too, unless the scope sets an `extensions` allowlist (`[]` ⇒ none). The statements dbd generates follow `source.dialect`: `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS` for PostgreSQL, a guarded `IF SCHEMA_ID(N'x') IS NULL EXEC(N'CREATE SCHEMA [x]');` for T-SQL, with every entity's DDL then closed by its own `GO` batch (SQL Server needs `CREATE VIEW`/`PROCEDURE`/`TRIGGER` first in their batch; a file already ending in `GO` keeps its own), nothing for MySQL/SQLite; PostgreSQL-only extensions and roles become a comment there. PostgreSQL output keeps `public` on a file's own path as `apply` does — after each top-level `SET search_path` (`SET LOCAL` and `= …` too) whose path leaves `public` out, a statement of its own sets the same path with `public` added, and no text of the file is changed — and puts `SET search_path TO <source.search_path>, public` ahead of a file that states none, as `apply` runs it — so `psql -f` on it behaves like apply. The statements are found in libpg_query's parse tree, so a function's `SET search_path TO ''` clause, a body, a string literal and a comment are never taken for one (before 0.25 `apply` rewrote the text with a regex, up to the next `;`: Supabase's `SET search_path TO ''` failed with `column "public" does not exist`, and a body returning `'g; ok'` came back `'g, public; ok'`). `-f` must resolve inside the project (a bare name against the project root; a path outside is refused). A file that does not parse is left out without a word — run `inspect` first.

### Exposed vs internal schemas

```yaml
schemas:
  - app:
      exposed: true     # PostgREST serves this
  - internal            # private (the default)
```

A table in an exposed schema is reachable by `anon` over HTTP. Internal unless
declared, except `public` on a `supabase` target. `exposed: false` overrides
that default; a bare name does not.

`dbd inspect` reports tables in exposed schemas with no RLS policy
(`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql`). Advisory — never changes the exit code.

A different axis from platform ownership: `extensions` is Supabase's and not
exposed; your own schema can be exposed without being Supabase's. Ownership
decides what `reconcile --prune` may drop; exposure decides what is readable
from outside.

### dbd emit

```sh
dbd emit --dialect mysql -f schema.mysql.sql
dbd emit --dialect tsql  -f schema.tsql.sql --report downgrades.json
dbd emit --dialect sqlite --scope hub -f hub.sqlite.sql
```

Translates the schema into **another engine's** DDL. Not `combine`, which
consolidates this project's own DDL into one script for its own target.

Targets: `mysql`, `tsql`, `sqlite`. The **source must be PostgreSQL** — it is
the only dialect dbd reads into columns and constraints, so emitting from a
T-SQL, MySQL or SQLite project is refused rather than producing an empty
schema.

`-f` and `--report` must resolve inside the project, as `dbml`/`diagram` outputs do —
a bare name resolves against the project root, and a path outside is refused
(`path traversal rejected: …`) rather than overwriting a file dbd does not own.

Tables — columns, `NOT NULL`, defaults, primary keys, unique constraints,
foreign keys and `CHECK` constraints (each with its `CONSTRAINT "name"` — a primary key's on SQL
Server and SQLite; MySQL names every primary key `PRIMARY`, reported), indexes, comments where the target keeps them,
identity/`serial` columns numbered by the target and generated columns computed by
it — and views/materialized views as `CREATE VIEW` (a matview becomes a plain view,
reported, and its indexes are left out, reported). On MySQL and SQL Server a view's
query and a `CHECK` expression are passed through untranslated and reported. On
SQLite both are written again from PostgreSQL's parse tree, node by node from what
SQLite has with the same meaning — `core.cities` reads `"core_cities" AS "cities"`,
`POSITION(a IN b)` becomes `instr(b, a)`, PostgreSQL's NULL order, `LIKE` escape and
result-column names are spelled out — and the first construct SQLite cannot run with
the same meaning leaves the view or CHECK out (and any view reading it), reported,
so the script applies; the output needs SQLite 3.39+. A rewritten statement is still
reported (the engines differ even where the SQL reads the same). A generated
column's expression is passed through untranslated and reported everywhere, and a
partial index's predicate on SQL Server and SQLite; an index the target would reject — an expression key
on SQL Server, a key on a column the target holds as unbounded text or binary (`text`, a `varchar`
with no length or past the target's limit, `bytea`, `json`) on MySQL or SQL Server — is left out and
reported, and MySQL builds a partial index over every row (reported). A key column
on unbounded text is bounded (`VARCHAR(255)`, `nvarchar(450)`), reported. A foreign
key to a table the script does not create (`external:`, out of scope) is left out,
reported. A file dbd could not parse is reported as missing. SQL Server gets
`CREATE SCHEMA` for every schema it uses and `CREATE SEQUENCE` with PostgreSQL's
bounds (`nextval` → `NEXT VALUE FOR`); MySQL and SQLite report each sequence, number
an integer key that drew from one with the table's counter, and drop other such
defaults — each reported. Functions, procedures and triggers — a trigger written in
a table's file included — are skipped and reported: their bodies are PL/pgSQL or SQL
that does not translate. Extensions, roles, grants (one entry per schema) and RLS
policies (one per policy file) are reported as not emitted. Enum types produce no
statement. A UNIQUE's `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` is reported as lost on MySQL and SQLite, whose
UNIQUE lets NULL keys repeat (SQL Server's UNIQUE already admits only one NULL key). A foreign key's
`DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` is carried to SQLite; an EXCLUDE constraint, a column's
`COLLATE`, a `MATCH FULL` foreign key and — outside SQLite — a deferred one are reported as
lost.

**T-SQL output ends every statement with `GO`** — the batch separator `sqlcmd` and
SSMS read; `CREATE SCHEMA` and `CREATE VIEW` must each be alone in a batch. `GO`
is not T-SQL: split the script on it before sending it through a driver.

Anything the target cannot express is **downgraded to the nearest thing it
can** — never a reason to refuse the whole schema — and each loss marked ⚠ below is reported. A loss appears
as a comment at the site in the emitted file — always one line, even when what it
quotes spans several (schema folds have no site, so they are in the summary and
report only; skipped routines, extensions, roles, grants and policies are noted where
the statement would have been) — and in the run's summary. `--report <file>` writes the same set as a JSON array of
`{entity, column, from, to, reason}` so CI can assert on the count.

Mapping (⚠ = reported; MySQL / T-SQL / SQLite): `text` and a `varchar` with no length →
`LONGTEXT` / `nvarchar(max)` / `TEXT` (MySQL's `TEXT` holds 64 KB); `varchar(n)` → `VARCHAR(n)`,
past 16,383 `MEDIUMTEXT`/`LONGTEXT` ⚠ / `nvarchar(n)`, past 4,000 `nvarchar(max)` ⚠ / `TEXT`;
`char(n)` → `CHAR(n)`, past 255 `VARCHAR(n)` ⚠ / `nchar(n)`, past 4,000 `nvarchar(max)` ⚠ / `TEXT`;
`bytea` → `LONGBLOB` / `varbinary(max)` / `BLOB`; `numeric(p,s)` → `DECIMAL(p,s)` clamped to 65
digits, 30 after the point ⚠ / `decimal(p,s)` clamped to 38 digits ⚠ / `NUMERIC` (⚠ when its
values can pass 15 significant digits with a fraction or 18 whole digits, which SQLite rounds); a bare `numeric` → `DECIMAL(65,30)` ⚠ / `decimal(38,10)` ⚠ / `NUMERIC` ⚠; a row wider
than the target stores has its widest non-key columns moved out of the row ⚠ (MySQL: to text,
65,535 bytes; SQL Server: `nchar` → `nvarchar`, 8,060 bytes); `text[]`/any array → MySQL `JSON` ⚠,
T-SQL `nvarchar(max)` ⚠, SQLite `TEXT` ⚠; `jsonb` → `JSON` / `nvarchar(max)` ⚠ / `TEXT` ⚠; `json`
→ `JSON` ⚠ (MySQL normalises the document) / `nvarchar(max)` ⚠ / `TEXT` ⚠; `uuid` → `CHAR(36)` ⚠ /
`uniqueidentifier` / `TEXT` ⚠; `timestamptz` → `DATETIME(6)` / `datetimeoffset` / `TEXT`;
`boolean` → `TINYINT(1)` / `bit` / `INTEGER`; `real`/`float4` → `FLOAT` / `real` / `REAL`; `time` →
`TIME(6)` / `time` / `TEXT` (a declared precision is kept); `timetz` → `TIME(6)` ⚠ / `time` ⚠ (the
offset is lost) / `TEXT`; `interval` → `VARCHAR(255)` ⚠ / `nvarchar(255)` ⚠ / `TEXT` ⚠;
`inet`, `cidr` → `VARCHAR(49)` ⚠ / `nvarchar(49)` ⚠ / `TEXT` ⚠; an **enum** or any other
type → `VARCHAR(255)` ⚠ / `nvarchar(255)` ⚠ / `TEXT` ⚠ (MySQL `ENUM` is not used and no
CHECK is added — the values are no longer enforced; the enum reason is given only for a
type the design declares as an enum, another type is reported as unmapped). MySQL and SQLite fold the schema into the name
(`schema_table`) ⚠; T-SQL keeps `[schema].[table]`. A name holding the target's quote
character is escaped as the target escapes it — SQLite doubles `"`, MySQL a backtick, SQL Server
`]` — where it ended the name early (`"app_we"ird"`) and the script did not run. Identity/`serial` →
`AUTO_INCREMENT` (⚠ for ALWAYS) / `IDENTITY(1,1)` (⚠ for BY DEFAULT and `serial`)
/ `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` (⚠ for ALWAYS); one the target cannot number
(not leading a key on MySQL, not a single-column integer key on SQLite) becomes a
plain column ⚠. Defaults: a literal loses its `::cast`; `now()`/`current_date` and
`gen_random_uuid()` are translated (MySQL's `now()` is `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(n)` at the column's
precision, its `UUID()` version 1 ⚠; on a `time` column `now()`/`current_time`/`localtime` is the
time of day — `(CURRENT_TIME(n))` / `CONVERT(time, SYSDATETIME())` / `CURRENT_TIME`); anything else
is left out ⚠. Comments: MySQL keeps table/column `COMMENT` (a view's ⚠), SQL
Server `MS_Description` on tables, columns and views, SQLite none ⚠. Still not
reported: an identity column's `START`/`INCREMENT` options; a lost time zone or length
(`timestamptz` → `DATETIME(6)` on MySQL, `TEXT` on SQLite; `varchar(n)` → `TEXT` on SQLite);
index keys past MySQL's 3,072 bytes or SQL Server's 900, which are not checked; SQL Server's
plain UNIQUE admitting only one NULL, where PostgreSQL's admits many; a foreign key named on its
column (`pid int constraint p_fk references …`), which loses its name; and a view's column list —
`CREATE VIEW v (a, b)` comes out with the query's own column names on every target. The MySQL
and SQL Server output is written from documented syntax, not run against a server.

```sql
-- dbd: `tags` was `text[]` — emitted as JSON; no array type exists here, so the `text` elements become a JSON document
`tags` JSON,
```

A *faithful* mapping is not reported. `integer` → `INT` loses nothing, and a
report padded with those is one nobody reads.

The exit status stays 0 when downgrades happen — they are the documented
behaviour, not a failure — which is why the count is what a pipeline should
assert on.

### dbd graph

```sh
dbd graph
dbd graph -n config.lookups             # subgraph from one entity
dbd graph --scope hub                    # filter to the 'hub' scope (composes with -n)
```

Output: `{ "nodes": [...], "edges": [...], "layers": [...], "scope": "hub" | null }`.
`scope` (v0.12.0+) names the scope the graph was narrowed to, `null` when
unscoped — in the JSON rather than beside it, since stdout is a contract here.
Every other command that takes a scope prints `scope '<name>': <kept> of <total>
entities` (`diff --json` on stderr); unscoped runs print nothing. A `-n`
that names nothing, or something outside the scope, is an error, not an empty graph, and so
is an `external:` name (dbd has no DDL for it, so it is no node of the graph), as `inspect -n`
and `apply -n` refuse one. Everything but the JSON goes to stderr — a file that does not parse
is named there (`⚠ … could not be parsed, so <entity> is left out: …`) and left out of the
nodes, layers and edges, as it says — and so is `-v`'s count — so `dbd graph -v | jq` parses.

### dbd diagram

```sh
dbd diagram                        # build the model and open the hosted interactive viewer
dbd diagram --print-url            # print the viewer URL instead of opening a browser
dbd diagram --site http://localhost:5173   # point at a different site (or set $DBD_DIAGRAM_URL)
dbd diagram --scope hub            # scope-aware (the scope's working set and its history)
dbd diagram --json -f schema.json  # write the raw SchemaModel JSON for upload/tooling
```

Opens the hosted interactive viewer at `https://dbd.sensei-hq.com/diagram` (root tabs Overview / Diagram / Entities (tables) / Changelog; per entity Details / Diagram / Changelog, enums Details / Changelog; a sidebar of every entity — tables, views, matviews, functions, procedures, triggers, sequences, enums — searchable and filterable by type — tables with fields (`IDENTITY`/`GENERATED` among the settings), references, dependencies, indexes with a partial index's predicate, Checks, a relationship diagram and their own changelog; views, routines and sequences with what they use and what uses them; enums with their values; a stub page — external, out of scope or unresolved — for a table a foreign key lands on that the model does not carry). The dbd-native schema model (schemas/tables/columns/FK refs) is gzip-compressed into the URL fragment — client-side only, never sent to a server, so the link is private and self-contained. `--print-url` prints the link without opening a browser (useful on headless machines). `--site`/`$DBD_DIAGRAM_URL` overrides the base URL. `--json -f schema.json` writes the raw SchemaModel JSON; drag the file onto the site's `/diagram` page (no file picker) or feed it to other tooling. The viewer keeps the designs you open in the browser's localStorage (`dbd:diagram:<project>`, listed and removable at `/projects`); nothing is sent to a server. The model carries `version` (currently `3`) and, being JSON rather than DBML, covers more than tables: `tables` (columns with `pk`/`nn`/`en`/`fk`/`uq`, type, default, comment, `identity` (`always`/`by default`) or `generated` (the expression), plus indexes with `where` for a partial one, and `checks` as `{name?, expression}`), `refs` (every foreign key — the ER edges, column-level as `{s,t,c}`), `stubs` (table-shaped nodes for the tables refs land on that `tables` does not carry: only the referenced columns, `kind` `external`/`out_of_scope`/`unresolved`; omitted when empty), `entities` (views, materialized views, functions, procedures, triggers — from the T-SQL/MySQL readers — and sequences), `deps` (what reads/writes/calls/uses what — the call graph; `uses` is a column's enum or sequence), `schemas` (every schema the model draws something in, with table and enum counts) and `project`. A `deps: include` scope whose closure needs what it excludes is refused rather than drawn empty; the viewer refuses a model newer than it reads. A DDL file that does not parse is left out of the model and named (`⚠ <file> could not be parsed, so <entity> is left out: <error>`), and the rest is still drawn — `Design::unparsed(scope)` lists them for an embedder. `entities`/`deps` are deliberately separate from `tables`/`refs`: an ER renderer wants FKs, a call-graph renderer wants dependencies, and folding them would change what every existing consumer of `tables` receives. A dep edge whose target is not a project entity (a built-in like `now()`, or a dangling reference) is marked `"unresolved": true` rather than dropped — the edge is real, only the endpoint is unplaceable. Comments reach the model for every kind, not just tables: `note` is the first line, `noteMd` the full text. `history` (v3, omitted when there are no snapshots) is what each snapshot changed, oldest first: the first a `baseline` of table/enum counts, each later one the tables and enums it added, removed or modified with their column, index, constraint and enum-value edits; a multi-stage rename or type change is one entry spanning `version`..`through` and reads as the rename or type change; type spellings are canonicalised; views, routines and sequences have no history (snapshots hold tables and enums only); under `--scope` it covers the scope's working set, the `deps: include` closure too. `enums` (v3, omitted when there are none) carries each enum type with its values in declaration order and its comment.

### dbd dbml

```sh
dbd dbml                       # writes design.dbml (when no dbml keys configured)
dbd dbml -f schema.dbml        # custom path; multi-doc keeps the directory, replaces filename
dbd dbml --scope hub -f hub.dbml      # document only the 'hub' scope's working set
dbd dbml --scope hub --deps include   # expand to the dependency closure first
```

When `design.yaml` declares multiple `dbml.<key>` entries, `dbd dbml` writes one file per key into the parent directory of `-f`, using each key's `output` (default `<key>.dbml`).

`--scope`/`--deps` are honored: the generated DBML covers the scope's working set (the closure under `deps: include`, the plain selection under `report`). `dbml` documents rather than deploys, so it does not gate on dependency gaps.

Every table a Ref points at that the document does not define gets a stub — a Ref to an undefined table is a DBML error — holding only the referenced columns, each typed like the foreign-key column that references it (else from the design, else `varchar`), with an `indexes { <cols> [unique] }` entry per referenced column set — so the SQL `dbml2sql` writes applies, a foreign key needing a unique key to point at — and a note: external, defined outside this document, or not defined in the project.

What DBML has no syntax for travels where DBML keeps it: CHECK constraints in a `checks { … }` block (backticked expressions, `[name: '…']` when named); expression index keys in backticks; a table-level UNIQUE as a unique index with its name and the note `unique constraint` (`(code, region) [unique, name: 'people_code_uq', note: 'unique constraint']`), read back by `init --from-dbml` as the named constraint; index notes with one fact per line — `where: <predicate>`, `order: <entry>, …` (`asc`/`desc`, optionally `nulls first`/`nulls last`, one per key; written only when some key is not plain ascending) and `nulls not distinct`, plus `include: <columns>`, `opclass: <entry>, …` (one per key, `-` for a key on its type's default) and `with: <name> = <value>, …` for `INCLUDE`, operator classes and storage parameters; an index's method as `type:`; a named primary key as a `pk` index entry with its `name:`, and a named foreign key as `Ref "name": …` — PostgreSQL's default names (`<table>_pkey`, `<table>_<columns>_fkey`) are left out, Postgres giving them back on apply; generated columns and ALWAYS identities as custom column properties (`generated always as: '<expr>'`, `generated as identity: 'always'` beside `increment` — a bare `increment` is BY DEFAULT). An enum column's type is written schema-qualified as the table's `search_path` resolves it, in DBML's own spelling of an enum (`app.mood`, or `"app"."mo\"od"` for a name that needs quotes), so the rebuilt DDL names a type that exists. Every name — schema, table, column, enum and enum value, index, primary-key, foreign-key, UNIQUE and CHECK names — is written in DBML's quoting and read back as itself, whatever it holds (a quote, a backslash, a space, a dot, a `'`, non-ASCII text; a schema, table or enum name also names a file, so a backslash in one is refused and a dot is not supported). Strings are escaped the way DBML's lexer reads them — an odd number of `"` in a `'…'` note included — and a column comment keeps its line breaks (DBML `\n`); a note that spans lines is written triple-quoted, which @dbml/core reads back exactly. A SQL value keyword default (`current_date`, `current_user`, …) is written as an expression (`` [default: `current_date`] ``), decided from its parse tree, not the string `'current_date'`. `checks` needs @dbml/core ≥ 5.0 and custom properties ≥ 9.1. `init --from-dbml` reads all of it back, a CHECK's name included (`CONSTRAINT "name" CHECK (…)`); a stub — recognised by its note — comes back as an `external:` entry, never a table to build (see reverse-engineering above), and a hand-written document is read as @dbml/core reads it. DBML has no syntax for a foreign key's deferral or `MATCH FULL`, an EXCLUDE constraint or a column collation, and the writer leaves them out, so they do not survive the round trip. An expression default or CHECK holding a backtick gives a document `init --from-dbml` refuses (DBML has no escape for one), and a line break inside a CHECK's or index predicate's string literal comes back as a space.

A DDL file that does not parse is named — `⚠ ./ddl/table/app/broken.ddl could not be parsed, so app.broken is left out: …` — and the document is still written, exit 0.

Per-doc options:

| Field | Type | Effect |
|-------|------|--------|
| `include.schemas` / `include.tables` | list | Only matching entities appear in this doc |
| `exclude.schemas` / `exclude.tables` | list | Removes matching entities |
| `output` | string | Output filename; default `<key>.dbml` |
| `auto_group_by_schema` | bool | Emit `TableGroup <schema>` for every schema in the filtered set |
| `groups` | list of `{name, tables}` | Explicit `TableGroup` blocks; names take precedence over auto-by-schema |

```yaml
dbml:
  base:
    exclude: { schemas: [staging] }
    auto_group_by_schema: true
    output: design.dbml
  core:
    include: { schemas: [config] }
    output: core.dbml
    groups:
      - name: lookups
        tables: [config.lookups, config.lookup_values]
```

Composite foreign keys (multi-column inline or table-level `ForeignKey`) emit DBML tuple syntax: `Ref: "schema"."table".("c1", "c2") > "schema"."other".("c1", "c2") [delete: cascade]`.

### dbd format

River-style DDL formatter. Operates on all `*.ddl` files in the project tree.

```sh
dbd format                     # rewrite files in place
dbd format --check             # exit 1 if any file would change (CI / pre-commit)
```

Driven by the optional `format:` section in `design.yaml` (falls back to defaults when absent):

```yaml
format:
  keyword_case: lower          # lower | upper | preserve
  comma_style: leading         # leading | trailing
  type_alignment: 27           # column for type start, 0 = off
  indent: 2
  query_style: river           # river (default) | none
  gutter: 10                   # river: width of right-aligned keyword column
```

`query_style: river` (the default) right-aligns keywords at `gutter`, leading-comma SELECT lists, alias/operator alignment, one condition per line. It applies to CREATE VIEW bodies + standalone SELECTs. Set `query_style: none` to disable river.

**`format` changes layout and keyword case, and nothing else.** Every rewrite reads the tokens PostgreSQL's own scanner produces (through libpg_query), so a string of any kind (`E'…'` with its escapes, `U&'…'`, `B''`, `X''`), a `$$`/`$tag$` body, a quoted name and a comment are each one opaque token. Statement boundaries are libpg_query's when the file parses (a `BEGIN ATOMIC … END` body is one statement); otherwise the scanner's `;` outside parentheses and outside the `BEGIN … END` body of a `CREATE TRIGGER`/`FUNCTION`/`PROCEDURE` (SQLite trigger bodies; a `CASE … END` inside does not close it). A keyword is recased where PostgreSQL's grammar reads it as one, and a word it reads as a name keeps its case even when it is a keyword elsewhere (a column named `name`, `value` or `level`); built-in type names are recased with the keywords. A statement's new layout is used only if it parses to the same libpg_query tree (sqlparser's, for a statement libpg_query cannot read) and every literal, body, quoted name and comment in it is byte-for-byte the same; failing that the statement is only recased, and failing that left as written. A file the scanner cannot read (an unterminated string or comment) is left unchanged. Before 0.25 hand-rolled scanners split `E'it\'s; tricky'` at its `;` and wrote it across three lines, split a `$tag$` body at its own `;`s and recased its `END`, and put an added `;` inside a trailing comment. Formatting twice changes nothing — `format` then `format --check` passes — and a comment beside a statement stays beside it, one above it above it (before 0.25 a comment after a last statement with no `;` was dropped, and one beside a statement moved to a line of its own). A table is laid out whatever its literals and names: a `U&'…'` or `$$` default, a quoted table or column name, a column's own CHECK, a named column constraint, and `TEMP`, `WITH (…)`, `PARTITION BY`, `INHERITS` or `TABLESPACE` around the column list. The layout is sqlparser 0.62's, so a table it cannot read is recased, not laid out: `UNLOGGED`, `LIKE`, `EXCLUDE`, `USING <method>`, `OF <type>`, `PARTITION OF`, identity options beyond one (`(START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1)`), a key's `INCLUDE`/`WITH`/`USING INDEX TABLESPACE`, `NO INHERIT`, `ON DELETE SET NULL (<columns>)`, a column's `STORAGE`/`COMPRESSION`, an `ARRAY` type (`int ARRAY`), `WITHOUT OIDS`, `U&'…' UESCAPE`; so is an enum type with a label holding a `'`.

All three `keyword_case` modes do what they say for every keyword in every statement: `preserve` leaves each keyword as written, and `upper`/`lower` reach `SET` and the column types of a table with a `serial` or `inet` column; comments, string literals, quoted identifiers and `$$`/`$tag$` bodies keep their text. `keyword_case` reaches every keyword the formatter writes — `GENERATED`, `ALWAYS`, `IDENTITY`, `STORED`, `MATCH`, `RESTRICT`, `ACTION`, `VALID`, `DATA` and every other keyword the grammar reads (`ATOMIC`, `COLLATE`, `BIT`, `PARTITION BY RANGE` …), the index methods (`btree`/`hash`/`gin`/`gist`/`spgist`/`brin`) and built-in type names (`bool`, `int2`/`int4`/`int8`, `float4`/`float8`, `bytea`, `timestamptz`, `timetz`, `json`, `jsonb`, `inet`, `cidr`, `money`) — so nothing keeps its case while its neighbours lose theirs. A word on the formatter's own list (`data`, `type`, `key`, `comment` …) is recased even where it names a column (`DATA JSONB` in `upper` mode). `format` and `inspect --fix` write each file back in the encoding it was read in: UTF-16 behind its byte-order mark stays UTF-16, a UTF-8 BOM is kept.

#### Pre-commit integration

`.pre-commit-hooks.yaml` at the repo root exposes two hooks:

- `dbd-format` — `language: rust`; pre-commit clones the repo at the pinned `rev`, runs
  `cargo install --path .`, caches afterward. **Needs v0.12.3 or later**: earlier tags
  have a virtual manifest at the repo root, so that install aborts with `found a virtual
  manifest instead of a package manifest` during environment setup, before anything is
  formatted. Use `dbd-format-system` with an older `rev`.
- `dbd-format-system` — `language: system`; expects `dbd` already on PATH (`cargo install
  dbd-cli`). Works at any `rev`.

Both set `pass_filenames: false` because `dbd format` scans the project itself. Consumers add to their `.pre-commit-config.yaml`:

```yaml
- repo: https://github.com/sensei-hq/dbd
  rev: v0.26.0
  hooks:
    - id: dbd-format
```

### dbd reset

Guarded by the bookkeeping environment check (`dbd.meta` on Postgres/Supabase, `_dbd_meta` on SQLite) **and** the scope guard (a wrong-`--scope` reset is refused unless `--allow-scope-change` or `--force`; see [dbd apply](#dbd-apply)). **Entity-level by default**: drops the
project's own objects individually — functions/procedures (every overload via a
`DROP ROUTINE` DO-block), materialized views (before the views/tables they read), views,
tables, sequences, enums — in reverse dependency order, with `CASCADE` on a full reset.
**A scoped reset never cascades**: `CASCADE` reaches past the scope (an in-scope enum took an
out-of-scope table's column with it), so it drops without it, all or nothing, and refuses
naming the dependents (`scoped reset refused, nothing was dropped — cannot drop type app.mood
because other objects depend on it: … add the dependents to the scope, or reset without
--scope.`); the policies and triggers on the tables and views it drops go first, with them,
so one calling an in-scope function (a `policies/` file, a trigger in its function's file)
does not refuse it. Never `DROP SCHEMA`/`DROP EXTENSION` by default, so `public`, custom schemas
and extensions (e.g. pgvector) survive and never abort on `public`; the next `apply`
repopulates the schemas.

```sh
dbd reset                    # Blocked if prod or version >= 1
dbd reset --force            # Override guard
dbd reset --dry-run
dbd reset --schemas          # also DROP SCHEMA for managed schemas
dbd reset --extensions       # also DROP EXTENSION for configured extensions
dbd reset --clean            # = --schemas --extensions
dbd reset --target postgres  # postgres | supabase | sqlite (default: the design's target key)
dbd reset --scope hub --dry-run   # only the objects the 'hub' scope occupies
dbd reset --allow-ownership-change  # run as this name although its entities here are all undeclared
```

Beside other projects, a reset drops only what its design declares and is refused, `--force` or
not, when another project depends on any of it; another project's `prod` record refuses an
unforced reset too. `--schemas`, `--extensions` and a full reset's roles keep what another project
has or uses, naming each (`schema app kept: it holds table app.invoices ("billing").`). See
**Sharing a database**.

`--target <postgres|supabase|sqlite>` selects the reset — and which schemas are protected from
`DROP SCHEMA` under `--schemas`. It defaults to the design's target key (the first `target:`
entry), so a Supabase project is protected without the flag; a design whose target has no reset
(Convex) is refused before connecting, and so is a target that is not the kind of database the
connection reaches (`reset: --target postgres does not match the database — the connection is
SQLite. …`), which was accepted and then failed on PostgreSQL's `CASCADE`. On `sqlite` the reset drops the project's tables and views
in one transaction with `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = ON` (the verbatim DDL gives no references to
order by), and `--schemas`/`--extensions`/`--clean` change nothing there and say so; on `supabase` the managed set (`public`, `auth`,
`storage`, `realtime`, `graphql_public`, `supabase_functions`, `pgbouncer`, `pgsodium`, `vault`,
`extensions`, `supabase_migrations`) is skipped; on `postgres` `public` is dropped, and every
role the design declares (`ddl/role/` and `target.roles`) is dropped on a full reset. The guards read the database: refused when it is
marked prod (rows written as `production` included) or versioned (`reset is blocked — the
database is versioned at v3. Use --force to override.`, with `(a released project's database)`
after `v3` only when `project.released` is set — it said "has applied migrations", even of a
fresh install that had run none), unless `--force`; after a `project.name` rename, the record the old name left counts (see
[Safety model](#safety-model)). `--dry-run` checks the same guards — prod, a versioned
database, the scope pin — whenever a
database is configured (`-d`, `DATABASE_URL`, or a `target.url` that resolves; an unset
`$VAR` does not), with `--force`/`--allow-scope-change` honoured the same way; a configured
database that cannot be reached fails to connect. With none configured it is an offline
preview.

Before the `DROP ROLE`s, reset revokes what `apply` granted those roles — the `schemas:`
and target `grants:` (USAGE, the table privileges, and the `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES`
entry set by the user running the reset) — on every schema that survives (a dropped
schema takes its grants with it). Roles are server-wide: a role another database on the
server holds anything in is kept and named (`Role reader kept: it holds privileges or
objects in database other — roles are server-wide, and dropping it would break that
database.`), its grants here still revoked; `--dry-run`, given a database, leaves its
`DROP ROLE` out and names it the same way. A role that still holds anything else here fails
the reset — which rolls back whole — with an error naming the role and what it holds
(`reset cannot drop role "x" — it still holds privileges or owns objects reset does not
revoke (it revokes only the schema grants design.yaml declares): …`); dbd never runs
`DROP OWNED BY`. Reset also deletes the `dbd.matview_stamps` rows of the matviews it
dropped and the project's recorded migrations, and a reset of everything the database was
built with — under the all-scope, or under the scope the database is pinned to (a design with a
`default:` scope builds and resets under it) — deletes the bookkeeping row — env, version, scope
pin — so the next apply records the database afresh: the way to rebuild as dev a database a run
without `-e` marked prod is `dbd reset --force`, then `-e dev`. A narrower scope keeps the row.

It prints what it dropped, counted by kind and read from the database before and after —
every drop is `IF EXISTS`, so the script cannot tell an emptied schema from one that had
nothing: `Reset dropped 1 materialized view, 1 view, 2 tables, 1 enum, 1 role (writer).` or
`Reset dropped nothing — none of the project's objects were in the database.`

`--schemas` additionally `DROP SCHEMA … CASCADE`s the managed schemas, always skipping
`pg_catalog`/`information_schema`/`pg_toast`; on a `supabase` target also skipping the
Supabase set (`auth`, `storage`, …, `public`), while on `postgres` `public` is dropped.
`--extensions` `DROP EXTENSION … CASCADE`s each extension in the target's `extensions:`
config — under `--scope`, only those the scope installs. `--clean` = both. `--scope` restricts the reset to the objects (and, with
`--schemas`, the schemas) the scope's working set occupies; roles are dropped only on a
full reset.

### dbd doctor

```sh
dbd doctor
dbd doctor --fix
```

Audits + migrates: old Node.js `design.yaml` format → new format (`--fix` writes a `.yaml.bak`); removes stale internally-managed files; migrates every non-canonical DDL type folder the scanner reads to singular (`ddl/functions/` → `ddl/function/`, `sequences`, and `materialized_views`/`matviews`/`matview` → `materialized_view`, merging into an existing singular folder, backing up the older file on a same-name collision as `<name>.ddl.bkp`). Also reports **misfiled view DDL** — a `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` under `ddl/view/` (which makes `reset` emit `DROP VIEW` on it) or a plain view under `ddl/materialized_view/` — with a move hint; `--fix` does not move these. And reports each `ddl/extension/` or
`ddl/schema/` file with the `design.yaml` entry it becomes (`./ddl/extension/citext.ddl → add
{ name: citext, schema: ext } to the target's extensions: list in design.yaml, then delete the
file`), which `--fix` leaves too; it counts what it fixed as it counts what it found
(`0 issues fixed, 3 left to fix by hand.`). Always exits 0.

---

### dbd install

```sh
dbd install                # install globally into ~/.claude (skills/ + agents/)
dbd install --project      # install into the current project's ./.claude instead
dbd install --dry-run      # preview what would be written, touch nothing
```

Installs dbd's Claude Code assets — the `dbd` skill (`skills/dbd/SKILL.md`) and the `dbd-pattern-verifier` agent (`agents/dbd-pattern-verifier.md`) — so an AI assistant working in the project understands the schema-as-code conventions. The assets are embedded in the binary, so this needs no repo checkout or network access.

Two scopes, and neither is system-wide (all OS users): **global** (default) writes under `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` if set, else `~/.claude`, and is personal to your machine across every project; **`--project`** writes `./.claude` (relative to `--source`), which is shared with the team only once you commit that directory (gitignore it to keep the install local to your checkout). Each asset is reported as created, updated, or unchanged — an overwrite on upgrade is never silent — and re-running is idempotent. Restart Claude Code afterwards to load the new skill/agent.

---

## GitHub source

`dbd deploy` is the only command that takes a GitHub source. Every other command
refuses one with a message — clone the repository and pass its local path.

```sh
# Shorthand
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database -d $DATABASE_URL

# With branch/tag
dbd deploy --source sensei-hq/daemon/database@v2.1 -d $DATABASE_URL

# Full URL
dbd deploy --source https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/main/database -d $DATABASE_URL

# GitHub downloads are cached under ~/.cache/dbd (macOS: ~/Library/Caches/dbd),
# keyed by owner-repo-ref and reused while a design.yaml is present.
# dbd deploy --no-cache re-downloads the current source;
# dbd deploy --clear-cache wipes the entire cache directory first.
```

For a private repository set `GITHUB_TOKEN`: dbd sends it as a bearer token to
`api.github.com` and nowhere else.

---

## Library usage

The guide page *Embedding dbd-core* (https://dbd.sensei-hq.com/guide/embedding)
covers the whole API; every example there is compiled by the test suite.
`Design::deploy` applies the configured grants like `dbd deploy` (reported as
`DeployComplete::grants`); `Design::apply_grants(adapter, scope)` applies them on
their own, scoped, returning a `GrantsOutcome` (`None`/`Applied`/`Unsupported`).
`Design::reconcile` does not check `project.released` — callers must.
`schema_model::build(&design, scope)` returns `Result<SchemaModel>` (a
`deps: include` closure needing what the scope excludes is refused).
`history::load_scoped(project_dir, keep)` takes a `keep(schema, name) -> bool`
predicate; `scope::admits(&scopes, &resolved, &working_set, &existing, qualified)`
is the one `dbd diagram` passes. `dbml::DbmlMultiParams` has a required
`design_entities` (the whole design, for typing stubs). `RefKind` has a `Uses`
variant (a column's type or the sequence its default draws from) — an exhaustive
`match` needs the arm. `DatabaseAdapter` gained `stamp_matview` and
`forget_matview_stamps` (no-op defaults) and `truncate_table` (default `TRUNCATE
TABLE`). `ImportPlanEntry.procedure` names only a procedure — one per staging table,
on its first entry; `design::import_entry_in_scope` is deprecated for
`Design::scoped_import_plan(name, scope)`, which also returns why each entry was left
out; `Design::live_import_plan(adapter, name, scope)` is that plan ordered by the database's
own foreign keys too — what an import runs, and what `import --dry-run` lists given a database. `Design::check_import_plan(name)` is every import refusal (a `-n` loading nothing,
`import.staging`, a loader tie), checked before connecting; `deploy` runs it before
applying. `Design::resolve_name(name, scope)` is the `-n` check, and
`Design::entities_to_apply(name, scope)` what `apply --dry-run` lists.
`Design::hook_skips(scope)` returns the `apply.*` hooks a run would skip, as the run
decides; `Design::unparsed(&scope)` the entities a generated document leaves out
because their files do not parse; the method `design.check_reset_guard(&marks)` the reset
guard (prod, a versioned database) a preview can run — a method, since its refusal calls the
database a released project's only when `project.released` is set. `ApplyComplete::previously_built` marks
a `Fresh` run on a database already built without a version; `Report` gained
`out_of_scope_warnings` (a scoped report's `warnings` hold only the scope's own);
`DeployComplete::policy_warnings()` is the policy phase's share of `warnings()`.
`DesignConfig::effective_schema_grants()` is what apply grants and reset revokes, and
`script::build_reset_script` takes that map as its final argument.
`source_text::read_with_encoding(path)` returns the text and its `Encoding`
(`Encoding::encode` writes it back), which `format` uses to keep a file's encoding.
Every guard reads a `DatabaseMarks` — `Design::database_marks(adapter)`: this project's
record, or, when it has none but the database holds this design's tables, views, matviews,
enums or sequences, the other projects' records (a renamed `project.name`), each refusal then
naming the project. **Breaking:** `Design::check_scope_guard(&marks, requested,
allow_scope_change)`, public since 0.24.1, took `Option<&ProjectMeta>`; wrap a row already held
with `DatabaseMarks::of_own(project, row)`. `Design::conflicting_pin(&marks, requested)` is its
decision, for a caller wording its own refusal. `Design::apply` checks the environment guard
(`Design::check_env_guard(&marks, env)`: a non-prod run on a database marked prod) and the
version guard (`Design::check_version_guard(&marks, design_version)`: a project older than the
database) — together `Design::check_apply_guards(&marks)` — before its first hook or write,
under `dry_run` too; `deploy`, `reconcile` and `import_data` check the env guard, and
`Design::guard_env(adapter)` (now public) is it for a load outside `import_data` or a preview.
`Design::env()` is the run's `-e`. `Design::pending_migration_preview(adapter, name, scope)`
returns the `MigrationPreview` `apply --dry-run` lists (steps in run order, `MigrationAction`
`Create`/`EnumValues`/`Migrate`/`Data`/`Drop`; `recorded` the versions a run records even with
no step, for a scoped run), and refuses a named apply over pending migrations as `apply` does.
`ExecutionStep` gains `AddEnumValues` (a version's enum value additions, committed ahead of the
rest of it) and `MigrateData` (its data scripts, after every schema change of the version) — an
exhaustive `match` needs the arms. `Design::search_path_warnings(name, scope)` is what `apply`
and `deploy` print for each file stating no `SET search_path`;
`Design::apply_hooks_to_run(scope)` and `grants_to_apply(scope)` what `reconcile --dry-run`
lists. `dbd_core::connect_existing(url, project)` (and `SqliteAdapter::open_existing`) is
`connect` for a caller that must not create a database — `None` for a SQLite file that is not
there. `Design::reconcile` runs the apply
hooks (`ReconcileComplete` gains `before_scripts`/`after_scripts`) but not the grants — call
`apply_grants` after it, as the CLI does. `Design::reset(adapter, target, force, schemas,
extensions, scope)` returns `ResetComplete` (`dropped` as `(kind, name)`, `count(kind)`,
`roles_kept: Vec<KeptRole>`); a reset under the all-scope or the database's pinned scope calls
`DatabaseAdapter::forget_project_meta` (a new required method); `roles_kept_by_reset` and
`reset_script_keeping` are the preview's halves, and `script::build_reset_script_keeping`/
`build_scoped_reset_script`/`build_sqlite_reset_script` the builders. `DatabaseAdapter` also
gained, defaulted: `existing_objects`, `roles_held_elsewhere`, `live_matviews`,
`other_projects_meta` (the rename guard's read), `execute_project_script(sql, search_path)` (a
migration or hook on its path), `matviews_reading_columns` (reconcile's enum-removal check),
`truncate_tables` (an import's tables emptied together), `dependencies` (`adapter::Dependency`,
what a scoped `init --from-db` names as needed) and `foreign_keys` (the keys between the
database's own tables, which order a SQLite import; none by default). `script::runnable_ddl(entity)` is a file's DDL as
apply runs it (`SET search_path TO <source.search_path>, public` ahead of a file stating none),
`script::runnable_script(sql, path)` a migration or hook script, and
`script::enum_value_additions`/`idempotent_enum_value_additions` the enum-value hoisting.
Structs gain fields a struct literal must set — `Entity.triggers`, `ColumnDef.collation`,
`ForeignKey.match_full`/`deferrable`/`initially_deferred`, `ReconcilePlan.destructive_changes`/
`enum_swaps` (`EnumSwap`), `ImportScan.unrecognised` — and `TableConstraint` gains `Exclude`
(compare definitions with `sql_expr::canonical_exclusion`; `reconcile::plan_exclusion_convergence`
is its pass). A key named on its column, or an inline `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, now parses to
the table-level `TableConstraint` it amounts to (a UNIQUE then without `is_unique` on the
column). For reverse-engineering: `reverse::SchemaSelect.supabase` (platform schemas left
out only on a Supabase source), `reverse::left_out_schemas`, `reverse::Declared` and
`design_yaml_with` (extensions and externals written into design.yaml), `reverse::outside_needs`
(the `needs:` lines), `reverse::keep_authored_triggers` (what `merge --from-dbml` keeps of a
table file: its triggers, each after its `SET search_path`), `scanner::is_env_folder`, and `doctor::detect_declared_kind_files`. `reconcile::plan_enum_recreation` reads indexes from the
snapshots it is given.

**Workspaces.** `Workspace::load(config, env, project_dir)` loads a design.yaml with or without
`modules:` (one without is a workspace of one module, named `None`); `Design::from_config_with_dir`
refuses one with `modules:`. `Workspace::select(module)` is what a run that builds or reads goes over
(the manifest's hooks attached), `select_alone(module)` `export`'s, `selected_to_reset(module)`
`reset`'s, `select_declaring(module, name)` `-n`'s; `under_scope(scope)` / `under_scope_of(scope,
module)` narrow to a scope's modules; `Workspace::locate(dir, config_name)` walks up from a module
folder; `Workspace::folders(config, project_dir)` lists the module folders without loading designs;
`design::check_scope_gaps(&modules, scope, deps)` is a run's gap check. A `Module` has `name()`,
`owner()`, `depends_on()` and `design()`; `Design::module()` and `Design::owner()` say whose a design
is. `Workspace::reading(module, scope, deps)` gives a `Reading` — the modules read as one design —
which `schema_model::build_reading`, `dbml::generate_reading` and `emit_dialect::emit_reading` take,
and which has `graph`, `combined`, `history`, `entities`, `declared`, `counts` and `module_of(name,
kind)`; a project's reading writes as `build`, `generate_all` and `emit_schema` do.
`config::update_version_of` / `set_released_of(config, module, …)` write a module's version and
release state. `split::plan_from_scopes(&design, renames)`, `split::write_split(&plan, config,
project_dir)` and `split::undo(project_dir)` are `dbd split`. `Design::retired_predecessor()` says
whether a run retired the project before it had modules (`Design::predecessor()` names it).

```rust
use dbd_core::{connect, ApplyComplete, Design};
use dbd_core::design::Progress;
use std::path::Path;

// Load the declarative design for an environment (sync; scans ddl/ next to the config).
let mut design = Design::from_config(Path::new("design.yaml"), "prod")?;

// Inspection — offline, no database. (`report` takes &mut self: it caches validation.)
let report = design.report(None, None);
// report.issues:              errors blocking the active scope (what apply refuses on)
// report.out_of_scope_issues: errored entities the scope excludes (non-blocking)
// report.warnings:            entities with warnings that the scope builds
// report.out_of_scope_warnings: entities with warnings the scope excludes
// report.gaps:                out-of-scope dependency gaps (when a scope is passed)

// Connect an adapter — Postgres/SQLite/Convex is chosen from the URL scheme.
let adapter = connect("postgres://localhost/mydb", &design.config().project.name).await?;

// Resolve the scope once (None, None ⇒ full design, the scope's default deps policy).
let scope = design.resolve_scope(None, None)?;

// apply / import_data take FIVE arguments: (&*adapter, name, dry_run, scope,
// progress). The three callbacks travel together in one `Progress` value —
// on_start(&str), on_done(&str, Option<&str>), on_complete(summary) — they are
// NOT three separate arguments. `Progress::none()` for a silent run.
// deploy drops the name and takes on_complete directly: (&*adapter, dry_run,
// scope, on_complete(DeployComplete)).
design
    .apply(&*adapter, None, /*dry_run*/ false, Some(&scope), Progress {
        on_start: |desc: &str| println!("→ {desc}"),
        on_done: |desc: &str, err: Option<&str>| if let Some(e) = err { eprintln!("✗ {desc}: {e}") },
        on_complete: |s: ApplyComplete| println!("applied {} entities", s.applied),
    })
    .await?;
design.import_data(&*adapter, None, false, Some(&scope), Progress::none()).await?;

// Or apply + import + policies in one call — the same pipeline `dbd deploy`
// runs, so an embedder and the CLI cannot drift. A failed policy file does not
// fail the deploy; it lands in s.policies.failed and in s.warnings().
design.deploy(&*adapter, false, Some(&scope), |s| {
    println!("v{} — {} table(s) imported", s.apply.to_version, s.import.tables);
    for w in s.warnings() { eprintln!("warning: {w}"); }
}).await?;
// Use design.deploy_with_progress(&*adapter, dry_run, scope, Progress { .. })
// for per-step callbacks (spinner / logging).

// Dependency graph (for visualization) — returns Result.
let graph = design.graph(None, None)?;
// graph.nodes, graph.edges, graph.layers
```

---

## Targets

| Target | Adapter | URL form | Extensions | Roles | SQL exec | Import | Migrations |
|--------|---------|----------|------------|-------|----------|--------|------------|
| PostgreSQL | sqlx-postgres | `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` | yes | yes | yes | COPY streaming (CSV/TSV, into the columns the header names); JSON/JSONL staged as `json` in the project's `dbd."import_tmp:<project>"`, moved by `dbd.import_jsonb_to_table` | `dbd.migrations` (dedicated `dbd` schema) |
| Supabase | sqlx-postgres (same adapter; the `supabase` key exposes `public`, protects Supabase schemas from prune/reset, adds PostgREST grants) | `postgres://…` (with `target: supabase`) | yes | yes | yes | COPY streaming | `dbd.migrations` (dedicated `dbd` schema) |
| SQLite | sqlx-sqlite | `sqlite://./app.db`, `sqlite::memory:`, `file:/abs/path` | no (errors) | no (errors) | yes | multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (?,?),(?,?), ...` batches in one tx (CSV/TSV/JSON/JSONL) | `_dbd_migrations` (SQLite syntax) |
| Convex | codegen | `convex:` (→ `./convex`; quote it in YAML), `convex://./out`, append `?deploy=true` to auto-deploy | no (errors) | no (errors) | no — `apply` writes `<dir>/schema.ts` | per-table via `npx convex import --table <name> --replace -y <file>` (always replaces — `truncate: false` has no effect; a `.json` must be an array); whole-deployment export via `npx convex export` (CLI has no per-table flag) | sidecar `<dir>/.dbd_state.json` |
| MySQL / SQL Server | **none** — `mysql://`, `mariadb://`, `sqlserver://`, `mssql://` refused by name | — | — | — | — | — | — |

### Adapter quirks

- **SQLite**: no schemas — `Schema` entities are silently no-op; entity names like `auth.users` resolve to the bare table `users` via `sqlite_master`. `Enum`/`Function`/`Procedure`/`Role`/`Extension`/`Sequence`/`MaterializedView` are rejected at apply time. No transactional apply; grants skipped; policy files fail; the import's truncate runs `DELETE FROM` (no `TRUNCATE`); CSV/TSV are read as RFC 4180 by header and exported as Postgres's `COPY` writes them, so files move between the engines unchanged; a SQLite project (`verbatim` reader) cannot `diff`/`reconcile`/`emit`; export writes `export/<table>.<fmt>` (the header even for an empty table, generated columns left out, a BLOB as `\x…` hex, which an import into a BLOB column decodes); an import loads a referenced table first and empties its tables one at a time, a referencing table first, in the order of the foreign keys the database reports (dbd's connections enforce foreign keys, and the verbatim DDL gives the design none); the shared data files sit directly in `import/` and env-only ones directly in `import/dev/`/`import/prod/`, loaded only under that `-e`; `reset` drops the project's tables and views in one transaction (`PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = ON`), and `--schemas`/`--extensions` change nothing.
    - **Offline ref classifier** — `classify_reference` checks an alphabetically sorted table of ~150 built-ins (aggregates, window/math/date/JSON1/scalar functions, type names) via `binary_search`, plus a `sqlite_*` prefix rule that catches all reserved system tables/views (`sqlite_master`, `sqlite_sequence`, `sqlite_stat1`, …). Everything else falls through to `UserDefined`.
    - **Trigger-aware DDL splitter** — `dbd format`'s statement splitter recognises SQLite `CREATE TRIGGER … BEGIN <stmts;> END;` blocks and keeps them atomic. `BEGIN` is only treated as trigger-body when the in-flight block already contains the `TRIGGER` keyword, so bare `BEGIN; … COMMIT;` transactions still split correctly. `CASE … END` inside the body doesn't trip the close detector — only `END` immediately followed by `;` at a word boundary closes the block.
    - **Batched imports** — `import_delimited` and `import_json_records` flush rows in multi-row `INSERT … VALUES (?,?),(?,?), …` batches sized by `batch_row_size(col_count) = min(500, 32000 / col_count)`. CSV uses a fixed header; JSON records (a JSON array or JSON Lines) detect column-set changes and flush the previous group before starting a new one. All inside a single transaction per import.
- **Convex**: codegen, not a SQL engine — `execute_script` returns an error (so `reset`, `policies`, grants, `diff` and `reconcile` are unavailable); only tables and enums are written, other entity types are skipped without a message; `apply_entities` is the canonical path (`prefers_batch_apply() = true`). Table names flatten `schema.entity` → `schema_entity` (Convex disallows `.`). SQL → Convex validator: `int*`/`numeric` → `v.number()`, text-like (`text`/`varchar`/`uuid`/`citext`) → `v.string()`, `boolean` → `v.boolean()`, timestamps → `v.number()` (epoch ms), `jsonb`/`json` → `v.any()`, `bytea`/`blob` → `v.bytes()`, `T[]` → `v.array(T)`, nullable → `v.optional(T)`. Indexes emit as `.index("name", ["col"])`. Convex platform columns `_id` / `_creationTime` are skipped if present.
    - **Enums** — an `Entity::Enum` named `config.status` with values `[active, inactive]` emits
      `export const config_status = v.union(v.literal("active"), v.literal("inactive"));` above
      `defineSchema`. Column whose `data_type` matches either the qualified name (`config.status`)
      or the bare name (`status`, case-insensitive) routes to that const; arrays become
      `v.array(config_status)`; nullable columns wrap in `v.optional(...)`.
