    - **Foreign keys** — single-column inline FKs (`ColumnDef.inline_fk`) and single-column
      table-level `TableConstraint::ForeignKey` whose target is a known table emit
      `<col>: v.id("target_convex_name")` (with `v.optional(...)` wrapping for nullable
      columns). Composite/multi-column FKs fall back to the scalar validator since Convex
      `v.id` only addresses one table.
    - **Auto-deploy** — `convex://./out?deploy=true` (or `ConvexAdapter::with_auto_deploy(true)`)
      runs `npx convex deploy` from the parent of the schema directory after `apply_entities`
      writes the file. Skipped when there were no entities to apply.
    - **Import** — `import_data(entity, null_value, dry_run)` shells out to
      `npx convex import --table <flat_name> --replace -y <file>`. `dry_run = true` logs
      the command and returns Ok without spawning. `truncate_table` is a no-op: `--replace`
      already empties the table.
    - **CLI dry-run** — `ConvexAdapter::with_cli_dry_run(true)` short-circuits all
      `npx convex …` invocations (deploy + import) to a stderr log line. Used in tests and by
      `dbd apply --dry-run` to avoid touching a live deployment.

---

## Reference cache (offline `inspect`)

`dbd inspect --from-db` runs `adapter.list_entities()` against the live database (via the `-d`/`--database` connection) — pulling every user-defined table, view, and enum (system schemas excluded) — and writes the snapshot to `<project>/.dbd/refcache.json`:

```json
{
  "captured_at": "2026-05-15T12:34:56Z",
  "source": "postgres",
  "entities": ["auth.users", "public.lookups", "config.user_role"]
}
```

Subsequent runs of `dbd inspect` (no `--from-db`, no `DATABASE_URL` needed) load this snapshot and drop any "Unresolved reference: NAME" warning whose target is in the set. Useful for CI, offline editing, or when the database is temporarily down. Commit the file to share with the team, or `.gitignore` it for purely local use.

API: `Design::write_ref_cache(adapter, source)` / `Design::resolve_unknown_refs_via_cache()` / `RefCache::{load,save,contains}` in `dbd_core::refcache`.

---

## Sharing a database

Several projects can deploy into one database. Each entity has one owner — the project whose
design declares it — recorded in `dbd.objects` (what each owner holds) and `dbd.uses` (what each
uses: schemas, extensions, roles, other owners' entities); on SQLite `_dbd_objects`/`_dbd_uses`,
an entity there being its name, schema-less and without regard to case. No run changes or drops
another project's entity:

- **Claim.** A run claims every entity its whole design declares (not its scope); declaring one
  another project holds is refused before anything runs, dry runs, `diff`, `import`, `refresh`
  and `policies` included. An `apply` in one transaction claims last, in it; `reconcile`, `reset`
  and `DBD_NO_TX` applies claim before their first write. A project's first run on this dbd claims
  what it declares that exists and nobody owns.
- **Prune.** `reconcile --prune` drops (a) a table this project owns and no longer declares, (b) one
  nobody owns in a schema no other project uses. One nobody owns where another project might —
  a schema another project uses, or any while a project has not upgraded — is kept, named, unless
  `--prune-unowned`. Another project's tables are hidden from `reconcile` and `diff`.
- **Uses guard.** Before anything is dropped — a table, column, constraint, index, enum value,
  schema or extension, by `reconcile`, a migration (`TRUNCATE … CASCADE` too) or `reset` — dbd asks
  what a `CASCADE` would reach and what other projects recorded using; anything another project
  depends on refuses the run, dry run included (`app.orders.total is used by "billing" (view
  billing.v_totals); remove that use first`). A dependent nobody owns counts where a project might
  own it (`… (owned by nobody; maybe by "billing")`).
- **Reset** keeps a schema (`--schemas`) holding anything not this project's or another project
  uses, an extension (`--extensions`) another project uses or depends on, and a role another
  project uses, with its grants; each named. Any project's `prod` record refuses an unforced reset.
- **Write lock.** Every `apply` (a `deploy`'s phases each), `reconcile`, `reset`, `import`,
  `policies` run and grant holds the database's dbd write lock — an advisory lock on
  `hashtext('dbd:write')`, taken with `pg_try_advisory_lock[_shared]`, polled every 100ms:
  exclusive for a reset, a reconcile and an apply running migrations, shared for the rest.
  `refresh` takes none. A run waits at most 5 minutes
  (`dbd: waiting for the write lock` in `pg_stat_activity`), then fails.
- **Name reuse.** A design under an owner name holding live entities it declares none of is
  refused (`owner "shop" here owns 1 entity (relation app.orders); this design declares none of
  them …`); `--allow-ownership-change` (apply, deploy, reconcile, reset) lets it run as that owner,
  passing the version guard but not the environment guard.
- **Transfer.** `--adopt-from <owner>` (apply, deploy, reconcile) takes over what the design
  declares that `<owner>` holds, in the claim's transaction, printing `adopting relation app.orders
  from "shop"` (a dry run: `[dry-run] would adopt …`); a third owner's entity still refuses the run.
  The giver's next run neither owns nor prunes it.
- **Workspaces** — the transfer rule. A module of a workspace takes over, as it claims, what it
  declares from its project's other owners: the project before it had modules (`<project>`) and the
  workspace's other modules (`<project>/<module>`, run or not) — as `--adopt-from` does, in the
  claim's transaction, said the same way (`adopting relation app.orders from "shop"`, `[dry-run]
  would adopt …`). An owner by any other name (`shopx`, `billing`) still refuses the run. What an
  entity uses goes with it, and its giver keeps those uses until the taker records its own. A module
  prunes nothing another module declares — it is moving there — and a reset keeps a schema holding
  such a table; a table moved between modules keeps its rows either way (T22). The project before it
  had modules is retired once its modules hold everything it held: its `dbd.meta` row, uses, claims of
  what is gone and matview stamps go, its migrations stay, and the run says `project "shop" is
  retired — its modules hold everything it held` (T24). A retire another session's open write holds
  up is left to a later run. Library: `DatabaseAdapter::claim_objects_from` (by default
  `claim_objects`, taking over from the one owner holding anything) and `retire_owner`.
- **`dbd inspect --shared`** reports each project, what it owns and uses, and this design's
  conflicts; non-zero over any. Library: `Design::shared_database`.
- **Onboarding.** `init --from-db` refuses only a database dbd manages for the project it creates;
  it and `merge` leave out other projects' entities, naming each, declaring `external:` what the
  new project depends on. Both refuse while a project has not run a dbd that records what it owns.
- **Limits.** Objects hook scripts create are unowned; roles are server-wide; an `apply` in one
  transaction runs `apply.before` hooks before its claim.

Full guide: https://dbd.sensei-hq.com/guide/sharing-a-database

## Safety model

The bookkeeping table records project name, environment, and version. On Postgres/Supabase this is
`dbd.meta` in a dedicated `dbd` schema (paired with `dbd.migrations` and `dbd.matview_stamps`, which holds each materialized view's drift stamp); the `dbd` schema is not in
PostgREST's default `db-schemas` (so it's unreachable via the API), and it's excluded from
reverse-engineering/`merge`/DBML/`diagram`/introspection and protected from `dbd reset`
(`--schemas`/`--clean` never drop it). Existing databases heal automatically — on the next
`apply`/`deploy`/`reconcile`/`reset`, dbd relocates the project's own rows of legacy
`public._dbd_meta`/`public._dbd_migrations` (and any scoped-apply strays in other schemas) into
`dbd.meta`/`dbd.migrations`; another project's rows stay, and so does a legacy table holding any
(that project may still be on an older dbd, and reads its record there until it heals), while an
emptied one is dropped; no user action required. On SQLite it's `_dbd_meta`/`_dbd_migrations` (SQLite has no
schemas, so the prefix is the namespace). Convex keeps migrations + meta in a JSON sidecar next to
`schema.ts`.

| State | `reset` | `reset --force` |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| dev, version 0 | allowed | allowed |
| dev, version >= 1 (`versioned at vN`) | blocked | allowed |
| prod (or a legacy `production` row), any version | blocked | allowed |
| another project's row prod (or an env dbd does not know) | blocked | allowed |
| another project depends on what it drops | blocked | blocked |
| fresh (no table) | allowed | allowed |

The environment is the one recorded by the last write, which can promote dev to
prod but never re-mark prod dev — a `-e dev` `apply`/`deploy`/`reconcile`/`import`
(and `import -n -f`, and each of their dry runs) against a database marked prod is
refused before it writes (the environment guard), since it would lift this guard and load
`import/dev/` data into production; there is no override. A run that promotes dev to prod
says so. `-e` defaults to `prod`, so a database applied without `-e dev` is prod; to
rebuild one that is not production, run `dbd reset --force` under the all-scope or the
scope the database is pinned to (it deletes the bookkeeping row), then `-e dev`.
`reset --dry-run` applies the same table whenever a database is configured, so a preview
refuses where the reset would.

**A renamed `project.name`.** The row is keyed on `project.name`, and more than one
project may share a database. Every guard read this project's row alone, so a renamed
project read a prod database as one dbd had never seen: `reset` with no `--force` dropped
its tables, a `-e dev` run passed the environment guard, an older revision the version
guard, another scope the pin. Now, when this project has no row but the database holds any of its tables,
views, materialized views, enums or sequences, the other projects' rows are the marks every
guard reads (unless the registry holds claims under this name, or what it holds there is being
adopted — neither is a rename) — each refusal names the project that set them and says to set
`project.name` back (`This database holds this design's objects but no record of project 'shop2'; it
records project 'shop'. dbd keys its record on project.name, so a renamed project.name is
the likely cause — if this design was 'shop', set project.name back to 'shop'.`). Two
projects sharing a database each read their own row — except that any project's prod mark
refuses an unforced `reset` — and a project the database holds nothing of is held to no
other's. Where the old name holds its entities in the registry, the renamed design is refused
for them, the refusal naming the rename (set `project.name` back, or `--adopt-from <old
name>`). Still a limit, in a database from before the registry: a renamed project whose run
trips no guard is recorded beside the old row, which stays; and a renamed design ahead of the
old row's version is planned as a fresh install, so its pending migrations do not run — set
`project.name` back before upgrading.

A project older than the database it is applied to — `project.version` behind the
database's, or none against a versioned database — is refused by `apply`, `deploy` and
their dry runs (`version guard: the database is at v3, but this project is at v2.`), since
re-applying older DDL over a newer schema is never right; there is no override, but for a
design `--allow-ownership-change` lets take over a reused owner name (the version recorded is the
previous design's).

---

## Environment variables

| Variable | Used by |
|----------|---------|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Default database connection — overrides `target.url`, overridden by `-d`; exported but empty, it does not override `target.url` |
| `$NAME` in `target.url` | A whole-value `url: $NAME` is read from the environment; unset or empty, it is refused by name with how to set it (`target.url is $DATABASE_URL, but DATABASE_URL is not set — export … or pass the URL with -d <url>`) |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | `dbd deploy` from a private GitHub repo — sent as a bearer token to `api.github.com` only |
| `DBD_DIAGRAM_URL` | Base URL `dbd diagram` opens (default `https://dbd.sensei-hq.com`); `--site` overrides |
| `DBD_NO_TX` | Set (any value) to apply without the single transaction |
| `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | Global install dir for `dbd install` (default `~/.claude`) |

The GitHub download cache is the platform cache dir + `/dbd`
(`$XDG_CACHE_HOME` or `~/.cache` on Linux, `~/Library/Caches` on macOS).

---

## Access control

Grants come from `schemas[].grants` and the first target's `grants` (any key),
merged per schema; applied by `dbd apply`, `dbd deploy` and `dbd reconcile` after the
schema (under `--scope`, only on the schemas it builds);
`usage` → schema USAGE, other perms → `ON ALL TABLES` + default privileges; plus
`NOTIFY pgrst`. Config grants cover schemas and tables — grant on functions or
sequences in an `apply.after` hook. On a `supabase` target, configured grants add
USAGE for `anon`/`authenticated`/`service_role` on every listed schema.
`exposed:` grants nothing; it drives `inspect`'s advisory "No RLS policy on N
table(s) in exposed schema(s)" report. RLS policies (`policies/<schema>/<table>.sql`):
`deploy` always (failure = warning, exit 0), `dbd policies` and
`apply --with-policies` (failure = exit 1), plain `apply` never.

## Other dialects and encodings

Readers: `pg_query` (PostgreSQL; structured), `tsql` and `mysql` (statement heads:
identity + references, no columns; the only readers that report triggers),
`verbatim` (SQLite: the file is the model). A T-SQL/MySQL project can `inspect`,
`graph` and `combine`; `diff`/`reconcile`/`emit` refuse; `dbml`/`diagram` show no
tables; `snapshot` records nothing; there is no adapter to apply to; `combine`
writes the schema statements in the project's dialect. DDL files are decoded from
UTF-8, or UTF-8/UTF-16LE/UTF-16BE with a byte-order mark, by every reader — scan,
apply, deploy, combine, format, doctor, merge and the migration readers; no mark and
not UTF-8 is an error naming the file. `format` and `inspect --fix` write a file back in
the encoding it was read in. Import data files are read as UTF-8 only.
